full_text:
(a) Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive. Evidence: the affected mother I-1 and unaffected father I-2 have both affected and unaffected children, consistent with aa × Aa; affected II-3 and unaffected known-carrier II-4 likewise produce both phenotypes. X-linked recessive inheritance is ruled out because I-1 is an affected female; if the trait were X-linked recessive, I-1 would be homozygous (XaXa) and would necessarily pass one Xa chromosome to EVERY son, making all of her sons affected — but sons II-4 and II-5 are unaffected, which is inconsistent with X-linked recessive inheritance. Dominant inheritance (autosomal or X-linked) is inconsistent with two unaffected parents (I-2, and II-4 "known carrier") producing affected children. Therefore the trait is autosomal recessive.
Genotypes (A = normal/dominant allele, a = disease/recessive allele): I-1 (affected) = aa; I-2 (unaffected father, must be a carrier because he and affected I-1 produced affected children) = Aa; II-3 (affected) = aa; II-4 (unaffected, given as a known carrier) = Aa.

(b)(i) Cross II-3 (aa) × II-4 (Aa) is a testcross. Punnett square: gametes from Aa parent = 1/2 A, 1/2 a; combined with aa parent's a gamete → offspring genotypes: 1/2 Aa (unaffected), 1/2 aa (affected). Probability the first child is affected = 1/2 (50%).

(b)(ii) Expected ratio for this Aa × aa cross is 1:1 (unaffected:affected). With 4 children, expected = 2 unaffected, 2 affected. Observed = 3 unaffected, 1 affected.
χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E = (3−2)²/2 + (1−2)²/2 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0.
With df = 1, χ²_crit = 3.84. Since the calculated χ² (1.0) is less than χ²_crit (3.84), we fail to reject the null hypothesis — the observed data are NOT significantly different from the expected 1:1 ratio; the small deviation is consistent with chance sampling variation given the small sample size (n=4).

(c)(i) The disease locus and marker M1 are 8 cM apart, so recombination frequency = 8%. In a coupling heterozygote (disease allele and M1 on one homolog; normal allele and m1 on the other) testcrossed to a doubly homozygous recessive individual, gametes from the heterozygous parent are: parental types (92% total, split 46%/46%) and recombinant types (8% total, split 4%/4%). Of 200 offspring:
• Parental class 1 (disease-allele phenotype with M1 marker present): 46% × 200 = 92
• Parental class 2 (normal phenotype, marker M1 absent): 46% × 200 = 92
• Recombinant class 1 (disease-allele phenotype, marker M1 absent): 4% × 200 = 8
• Recombinant class 2 (normal phenotype, marker M1 present): 4% × 200 = 8
(Total = 200.)

(c)(ii) If the two genes were unlinked (on different chromosomes or far enough apart to assort independently), independent assortment during meiosis I would randomize allele combinations equally, producing an expected 1:1:1:1 ratio (50 offspring per class) regardless of parental combinations. Because these genes ARE linked (only 8 cM apart), the two alleles that started out together on the same parental homolog (coupling) are transmitted together far more often than not, since separating them requires a crossover event between the loci, which happens in only ~8% of meioses. This produces a large excess of parental-type offspring (92 each) relative to recombinant types (8 each), sharply deviating from the 1:1:1:1 ratio expected under independent assortment.

(d) Normally, meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (one maternal, one paternal homolog) into different secondary cells, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids (genetically identical copies produced by DNA replication of a single homolog) into different gametes. If nondisjunction occurs during meiosis II -- sister chromatids of chromosome 7 fail to separate at anaphase II -- one resulting gamete receives both (identical) sister-chromatid copies of chromosome 7, making it disomic (n+1) for chromosome 7, while the other resulting gamete receives no copy of chromosome 7 (n-1). When the n+1 gamete (carrying two copies of chromosome 7) is fertilized by a normal gamete (carrying one copy of chromosome 7), the resulting zygote has three total copies of chromosome 7 -- it is trisomic for chromosome 7 (2n+1), one chromosome more than the normal diploid number.

Because these genes ARE linked (only 8 cM apart), the two alleles that started out together on the same parental homolog (coupling) are transmitted together far more often than not, since separating them requires a crossover event between the loci, which happens in only ~8% of meioses. This produces a large excess of parental-type offspring (92 each) relative to recombinant types (8 each), sharply deviating from the 1:1:1:1 ratio expected under independent assortment.

derivations.expression: (d) Normally, meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (one maternal, one paternal homolog) into different secondary cells, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids (genetically identical copies produced by DNA replication of a single homolog) into different gametes. If nondisjunction occurs during meiosis II -- sister chromatids of chromosome 7 fail to separate at anaphase II -- one resulting gamete receives both (identical) sister-chromatid copies of chromosome 7, making it disomic (n+1) for chromosome 7, while the other resulting gamete receives no copy of chromosome 7 (n-1). When the n+1 gamete (carrying two copies of chromosome 7) is fertilized by a normal gamete (carrying one copy of chromosome 7), the resulting zygote has three total copies of chromosome 7 -- it is trisomic for chromosome 7 (2n+1), one chromosome more than the normal diploid number.

full_text:
(a) In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, E. coli were grown for many generations in medium containing heavy nitrogen (15N) as the sole nitrogen source, so that all newly synthesized DNA incorporated 15N into its nitrogenous bases, producing uniformly "heavy" DNA. Cells were then transferred to medium containing only light nitrogen (14N), and DNA was extracted after each round of replication (generation). DNA samples were separated by cesium chloride (CsCl) density-gradient centrifugation, which separates DNA molecules by density. Results: after one generation, all DNA banded at a single, intermediate density — halfway between pure heavy (15N/15N) and pure light (14N/14N) DNA. After two generations, DNA showed two bands: one at the intermediate density and one at the fully light density, present in equal amounts. This pattern supports the semiconservative model: the intermediate band after generation 1 shows each new DNA duplex contains one old (heavy) strand paired with one new (light) strand — ruling out the conservative model, which predicts that after one generation there would be one fully heavy band (the original parental duplex, intact) and one fully light band (an entirely new duplex), never an intermediate band. The appearance of a fully light band after the second generation (from a duplex whose original heavy strand was paired with light in generation 1, then that light strand served as template for another light strand) together with a persisting intermediate band rules out the dispersive model, which predicts that DNA would remain as a single band of progressively decreasing (but never purely light) density each generation, since old and new DNA would be randomly interspersed throughout every molecule.

(b)(i) Helicase: unwinds the parental DNA double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs at the replication fork, generating the single-stranded template DNA needed for replication; necessary because DNA polymerase can only synthesize using single-stranded template.
(ii) DNA primase: synthesizes a short RNA primer complementary to the template strand, providing a free 3'-OH group to which new nucleotides can be added; necessary because DNA polymerases cannot initiate synthesis de novo — they can only extend an existing strand from a free 3'-OH.

Template position 8 (C) pairs with mRNA position 8 (G); after the template C->T mutation, the complementary mRNA base becomes A (T pairs with A), so mRNA codon 3 changes from GGA (Gly) to GAA (Glutamate, Glu). derivations.expression: (d) Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases catalyze the covalent attachment ("charging") of each amino acid to the 3' CCA end of its correct, cognate tRNA, using ATP. If a drug blocks this enzyme activity, tRNAs can no longer be charged with their amino acids. Without charged (aminoacyl-) tRNAs available, ribosomes have no amino acids to deliver to the A site during translation, so the addition of new amino acids to a growing polypeptide chain cannot occur — protein synthesis (translation) would be halted globally across the cell. Existing proteins already made would remain functional in the short term, but the cell would be unable to synthesize any new proteins (needed to replace degraded/short-lived proteins, respond to signals, replicate, or carry out normal cellular functions), which would ultimately be lethal to the cell.

full_text:
(a) Mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm (1976, pre-drought) to 9.96 mm in drought survivors, and remained elevated at 10.07 mm by 1978. This reflects natural selection acting on pre-existing heritable variation in beak depth within the finch population (source of variation: beak depth varies among individual finches due to underlying genetic differences, i.e., standing genetic variation, prior to the drought). The selective agent was the drought-induced scarcity of small, soft seeds, which left only large, hard seeds available; birds needed sufficiently deep, strong beaks to crack these large hard seeds. This produced differential survival: only 85 of 642 birds survived the drought, and the survivors had a significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population mean (9.42 mm) — individuals with deeper beaks were better able to access/process the remaining large hard seeds and thus survived and reproduced at higher rates than shallow-beaked individuals. Because beak depth is heritable (passed from parents to offspring via genes), the surviving (deeper-beaked) birds' offspring inherited genes for deeper beaks, so the population's mean beak depth remained elevated (10.07 mm) into the next generation (1978) — this shift in the population's genetic/phenotypic composition, resulting from differential reproductive success of individuals with a heritable advantageous trait, is natural selection.

(b) Given allele frequencies p (allele D) = 0.6 and q (allele d) = 0.4, expected genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium are: DD = p² = 0.36, Dd = 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48, dd = q² = 0.16. Observed genotype frequencies in 1976 (N=642) were: DD = 0.40, Dd = 0.42, dd = 0.18. Converting to counts: Expected counts — DD = 0.36×642 = 231.1, Dd = 0.48×642 = 308.2, dd = 0.16×642 = 102.7. Observed counts — DD = 0.40×642 ≈ 257, Dd = 0.42×642 ≈ 270, dd = 0.18×642 ≈ 116.
χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E = (257−231.1)²/231.1 + (270−308.2)²/308.2 + (116−102.7)²/102.7
= (25.9)²/231.1 + (−38.2)²/308.2 + (13.3)²/102.7
= 670.8/231.1 + 1459.2/308.2 + 176.9/102.7
≈ 2.90 + 4.73 + 1.72 = 9.35
With df = 1 (3 genotype classes − 1 − 1 estimated allele frequency parameter) and χ²_crit = 3.84 (p=0.05), the calculated χ² (9.35) exceeds χ²_crit (3.84), so we reject the null hypothesis of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium — the observed genotype frequencies deviate significantly from HWE expectations, meaning the 1976 population was NOT in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this locus (consistent with ongoing natural selection/nonrandom mating rather than the idealized HWE assumptions of no selection, random mating, no migration, no mutation, and infinite population size).

(c)(i) After the 1983 El Niño, small soft seeds became abundant, and mean beak depth shifted back toward smaller values by 1984 — this is directional selection (selection favoring one phenotypic extreme, shifting the population mean in one direction), here favoring SMALLER beak depth. Small, soft seeds require less force to crack open, so finches with smaller, more slender beaks could feed on them efficiently (with less energy expenditure/handling time) than deep-beaked finches, which are specialized for large, hard seeds but are less efficient at processing small soft seeds; with small soft seeds now abundant, smaller-beaked birds had a survival/foraging advantage, so directional selection shifted the population mean toward smaller beak depth.

(c)(ii) This shift does NOT represent Lamarckian inheritance because no individual bird's beak physically changed in response to use or environmental conditions during its own lifetime and then passed that acquired change to offspring (which is what Lamarckian "inheritance of acquired characteristics" would require). Instead, the shift reflects a change in the population's allele frequencies due to natural selection acting on pre-existing heritable genetic variation: individuals that already happened to carry alleles for smaller beak depth had higher relative survival/reproduction under the new (post-El Niño) conditions, so those alleles increased in frequency in the next generation. The mechanism is differential reproductive success of pre-existing genotypes, not modification of an individual's traits during its lifetime followed by inheritance of that modification.

(d) The competitive exclusion principle states that two species cannot indefinitely coexist in the same community if they compete for exactly the same limiting resource(s) in the same way, because the more efficient competitor will eventually outcompete and exclude the other from that shared niche. G. magnirostris, with its larger beak, is a superior competitor for large, hard seeds compared to the medium ground finch. As G. magnirostris establishes itself on Daphne Major and competes for this same large-seed resource, medium ground finches (especially those individuals with larger beak depths, most similar in diet/niche to G. magnirostris) may experience increased competition for large seeds, potentially reducing their survival and reproductive success and causing a decline in the medium ground finch population (or at least in its large-beaked segment). A possible evolutionary outcome allowing coexistence is character displacement: natural selection could favor medium ground finches with smaller beak depths (shifting the population's beak-depth distribution away from overlap with G. magnirostris), resulting in niche partitioning where medium ground finches specialize increasingly on smaller seeds while G. magnirostris specializes on larger seeds — reducing direct resource competition and allowing the two species to coexist on the island.

Because beak depth is heritable (passed from parents to offspring via genes), the surviving (deeper-beaked) birds' offspring inherited genes for deeper beaks, so the population's mean beak depth remained elevated (10.07 mm) into the next generation (1978) — this shift in the population's genetic/phenotypic composition, resulting from differential reproductive success of individuals with a heritable advantageous trait, is natural selection.

full_text:
(a)(i) Graph description: percent mass change starts strongly positive (+8.4%) at 0 M sucrose and decreases progressively (in a roughly linear, downward-sloping trend) as sucrose concentration increases, crossing from positive to negative between 0.3 M (+0.2%) and 0.4 M (−0.2%), and continuing to decline to a strongly negative value (−15.8%) at 0.8 M. Key points to label: the y-intercept at (0 M, +8.4%), the x-intercept (zero mass change) at approximately 0.35 M, and the endpoint at (0.8 M, −15.8%).

(a)(ii) The sucrose concentration at osmotic equilibrium (0% mass change) falls between 0.3 M (+0.2%) and 0.4 M (−0.2%); interpolating, this is approximately 0.35 M. This tells us that the internal solute concentration of the potato tissue is approximately 0.35 M (in sucrose-equivalent terms) — at this external concentration, water has no net tendency to move into or out of the cells because the internal and external solute (and thus water potential) concentrations are equal.

(a)(iii) At 0.2 M sucrose, the external solution (0.2 M) is hypotonic relative to the potato tissue (whose internal solute concentration is ~0.35 M) — the potato cells have a higher internal solute concentration than the surrounding solution. Net water movement will be INTO the potato cells, down the water potential gradient from the more dilute external solution (higher Ψ) to the more concentrated cell interior (lower Ψ), consistent with the observed mass gain (+1.6%). As water enters, the cells become more turgid: the protoplast swells and presses against the cell wall, increasing turgor pressure, but the rigid cell wall prevents lysis.

(b)(i) Water potential (Ψ) is a measure of the free energy of water per unit volume/area, which determines the direction water will move (water moves from regions of higher Ψ to regions of lower Ψ); it is measured in pressure units (bars or MPa). Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, where Ψs (solute potential/osmotic potential) is the reduction in water potential caused by dissolved solutes (always ≤ 0, since solutes reduce the free energy/entropy available to water), and Ψp (pressure potential) is the physical pressure exerted on the water — in plant cells this is typically the turgor pressure created by the protoplast pushing against the rigid cell wall (positive when the cell is turgid).

(b)(ii) The potato tissue's Ψs = −7.0 bars. Placed in pure water, Ψ(outside) = 0 bars (Ψs = 0, Ψp = 0 for pure water). At equilibrium, water potential inside the cell equals water potential outside: Ψ(inside) = Ψ(outside) → Ψs + Ψp = 0 → (−7.0) + Ψp = 0 → Ψp = +7.0 bars. This positive pressure potential represents the turgor pressure built up inside the cell as water enters and the protoplast presses against the cell wall; the wall pushes back with an equal, opposing pressure. At equilibrium, this turgor pressure exactly counterbalances the tendency of water to keep entering due to the cell's negative solute potential (even though a concentration difference in solutes still exists), so net water movement stops — the cell is fully turgid.

(c) Hypotonic solution: Plant cell — water moves INTO the cell (down the water potential gradient, since the hypotonic solution has a higher Ψ than the cell); the rigid cellulose cell wall prevents the cell from bursting by generating counter (pressure) potential, so the cell becomes turgid (firm), which is beneficial for structural support. Animal cell (e.g., RBC) — water moves into the cell, but with no rigid wall to resist expansion and build counter-pressure, the cell can swell uncontrollably and undergo lysis (membrane rupture).
Hypertonic solution: Plant cell — water moves OUT of the cell (toward the lower-Ψ hypertonic external solution); the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the rigid cell wall, a process called plasmolysis, and the cell becomes flaccid (loses turgor). Animal cell — water moves out and the cell shrinks/shrivels, a process called crenation.

(d)(i) Aquaporins are channel proteins that form water-permeable pores across the membrane, allowing water molecules to cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer much more rapidly (facilitated diffusion) than by unassisted diffusion through the membrane alone. Aquaporins do not use ATP and cannot move water against its water-potential gradient — they simply provide a faster, lower-resistance pathway for water to move down the SAME gradient (from high Ψ to low Ψ) that would drive movement anyway. Because movement is still occurring passively down an existing free-energy gradient (aquaporins only increase the rate/permeability, not the direction or the thermodynamic favorability of movement), the process remains passive osmosis, not active transport.

(d)(ii) A cell with reduced/deleted aquaporin expression placed in a hypertonic solution will still lose water — net water movement will still be OUT of the cell, since the direction is dictated by the water potential gradient (unchanged by aquaporin presence) — but the RATE of water loss (and thus the rate of plasmolysis) will be SLOWER than in a normal cell, because water must now cross the membrane primarily via slow diffusion through the lipid bilayer itself rather than through the fast aquaporin channels. The final equilibrium extent of plasmolysis would eventually be similar to a normal cell, but the aquaporin-deficient cell would take longer to reach that equilibrium state.

(b)(i) Water potential (Ψ) is a measure of the free energy of water per unit volume/area, which determines the direction water will move (water moves from regions of higher Ψ to regions of lower Ψ); it is measured in pressure units (bars or MPa). Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, where Ψs (solute potential/osmotic potential) is the reduction in water potential caused by dissolved solutes (always ≤ 0, since solutes reduce the free energy/entropy available to water), and Ψp (pressure potential) is the physical pressure exerted on the water — in plant cells this is typically the turgor pressure created by the protoplast pushing against the rigid cell wall (positive when the cell is turgid).

(b)(ii) The potato tissue's Ψs = −7.0 bars. Placed in pure water, Ψ(outside) = 0 bars (Ψs = 0, Ψp = 0 for pure water). At equilibrium, water potential inside the cell equals water potential outside: Ψ(inside) = Ψ(outside) → Ψs + Ψp = 0 → (−7.0) + Ψp = 0 → Ψp = +7.0 bars. This positive pressure potential represents the turgor pressure built up inside the cell as water enters and the protoplast presses against the cell wall; the wall pushes back with an equal, opposing pressure. At equilibrium, this turgor pressure exactly counterbalances the tendency of water to keep entering due to the cell's negative solute potential (even though a concentration difference in solutes still exists), so net water movement stops — the cell is fully turgid.

(c) Hypotonic solution: Plant cell — water moves INTO the cell (down the water potential gradient, since the hypotonic solution has a higher Ψ than the cell); the rigid cellulose cell wall prevents the cell from bursting by generating counter (pressure) potential, so the cell becomes turgid (firm), which is beneficial for structural support. Animal cell (e.g., RBC) — water moves into the cell, but with no rigid wall to resist expansion and build counter-pressure, the cell can swell uncontrollably and undergo lysis (membrane rupture).
Hypertonic solution: Plant cell — water moves OUT of the cell (toward the lower-Ψ hypertonic external solution); the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the rigid cell wall, a process called plasmolysis, and the cell becomes flaccid (loses turgor). Animal cell — water moves out and the cell shrinks/shrivels, a process called crenation.

(d)(i) Aquaporins are channel proteins that form water-permeable pores across the membrane, allowing water molecules to cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer much more rapidly (facilitated diffusion) than by unassisted diffusion through the membrane alone. Aquaporins do not use ATP and cannot move water against its water-potential gradient — they simply provide a faster, lower-resistance pathway for water to move down the SAME gradient (from high Ψ to low Ψ) that would drive movement anyway. Because movement is still occurring passively down an existing free-energy gradient (aquaporins only increase the rate/permeability, not the direction or the thermodynamic favorability of movement), the process remains passive osmosis, not active transport.

(d)(ii) A cell with reduced/deleted aquaporin expression placed in a hypertonic solution will still lose water — net water movement will still be OUT of the cell, since the direction is dictated by the water potential gradient (unchanged by aquaporin presence) — but the RATE of water loss (and thus the rate of plasmolysis) will be SLOWER than in a normal cell, because water must now cross the membrane primarily via slow diffusion through the lipid bilayer itself rather than through the fast aquaporin channels. The final equilibrium extent of plasmolysis would eventually be similar to a normal cell, but the aquaporin-deficient cell would take longer to reach that equilibrium state.

full_text:
(a) From Table 1, reaction rate approaches an asymptote near 50 μmol/min at high substrate concentrations (49.5–50.0 μmol/min at [S] = 1000–5000 μM), so Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min. Km is the substrate concentration at which reaction rate equals half of Vmax (25 μmol/min); the table shows rate = 25 μmol/min occurs exactly at [S] = 40 μM, so Km ≈ 40 μM.
Biological significance: Km is inversely related to the enzyme's apparent affinity for its substrate — a LOW Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at a low substrate concentration, indicating HIGH affinity (the enzyme binds and processes substrate effectively even when substrate is scarce); a HIGH Km indicates lower affinity (more substrate is needed to achieve the same fractional saturation). Vmax reflects the maximum catalytic capacity of the enzyme population under the given conditions, once the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate — it depends on the total amount/concentration of enzyme present and each enzyme molecule's intrinsic turnover number (kcat, how quickly an individual enzyme molecule converts bound substrate to product).

(b)(i) Inhibitor A: Vmax unchanged (50, same as no inhibitor) but Km increased (120 vs. 40) → classified as a COMPETITIVE inhibitor. A higher apparent Km means more substrate is required to reach half-maximal velocity, consistent with the inhibitor competing with substrate for the same binding site — but because sufficiently high substrate concentration can still outcompete the inhibitor, the same Vmax can eventually be reached.
Inhibitor B: Vmax decreased (25 vs. 50) but Km unchanged (40, same as no inhibitor) → classified as a NONCOMPETITIVE inhibitor. Vmax is reduced because a fraction of enzyme molecules is rendered nonfunctional regardless of substrate concentration, but the affinity (Km) of the remaining active enzyme for substrate is unaffected, since this inhibitor does not compete at the active site.

(b)(ii) Competitive inhibitor (A): binds reversibly to the enzyme's active site itself, typically because it structurally resembles the substrate, physically blocking the substrate from binding there. Because this competition is reversible and concentration-dependent, sufficiently high substrate concentrations can outcompete/displace the inhibitor from the active site, so the reaction can still eventually reach the same Vmax as uninhibited enzyme (just requiring more substrate — a higher apparent Km).
Noncompetitive inhibitor (B): binds to a site on the enzyme distinct from the active site (an allosteric site), inducing a conformational change that impairs or abolishes the enzyme's catalytic activity regardless of how much substrate is bound. Because it does not compete with substrate for the active site, increasing substrate concentration cannot reverse this inhibition — the Vmax of the enzyme population is reduced (some fraction of enzyme is nonfunctional at any time), while the Km (affinity) of the still-active, uninhibited enzyme molecules remains unchanged.

(c) Threonine deaminase catalyzes the first committed step of the pathway converting threonine to isoleucine. Isoleucine, the pathway's end product, binds threonine deaminase at an allosteric site — a regulatory binding site physically and structurally distinct from the active site, where threonine itself binds and is chemically converted. When isoleucine binds this allosteric site, it induces a conformational change that is transmitted through the enzyme's tertiary/quaternary structure to the active site, distorting its shape so that it can no longer efficiently bind threonine or catalyze the reaction — reducing enzyme activity. This is feedback inhibition (end-product inhibition): the pathway's own final product inhibits an enzyme earlier in its own biosynthetic pathway, creating a self-regulating mechanism — as isoleucine accumulates to sufficient levels, it shuts down further isoleucine production by inhibiting threonine deaminase, preventing wasteful overproduction; as isoleucine is consumed/depleted, inhibition is relieved and the pathway resumes.

(d)(i) From 0°C up to the temperature optimum, increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of enzyme and substrate molecules, increasing both the frequency and the energy of molecular collisions between them; this increases the rate at which enzyme–substrate complexes form and successfully proceed to products, so reaction rate increases with temperature in this range.
(d)(ii) Above the temperature optimum, reaction rate decreases sharply because excess thermal energy disrupts the weak, noncovalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that maintain the enzyme's precise tertiary/quaternary structure. The enzyme begins to denature (unfold from its native, catalytically functional conformation), progressively distorting or destroying the specific shape of the active site required for substrate binding and catalysis, so catalytic activity falls off rapidly as an increasing fraction of enzyme molecules become permanently denatured and nonfunctional.
(d)(iii) A thermophilic bacterium's enzyme would likely have structural features that create MORE and/or stronger stabilizing interactions holding its tertiary/quaternary structure together — e.g., more ionic bonds/salt bridges, more hydrogen bonds, more disulfide bonds, and/or tighter hydrophobic core packing — than the equivalent mesophilic enzyme. These additional stabilizing interactions allow the thermophilic protein to resist thermal denaturation and maintain its functional 3D conformation (and active-site shape) at the higher temperatures characteristic of the thermophile's environment, whereas the mesophilic enzyme's comparatively fewer/weaker stabilizing interactions cause it to denature at the lower temperatures typical of mesophilic environments.

Km is the substrate concentration at which reaction rate equals half of Vmax (25 μmol/min); the table shows rate = 25 μmol/min occurs exactly at [S] = 40 μM, so Km ≈ 40 μM.
Biological significance: Km is inversely related to the enzyme's apparent affinity for its substrate — a LOW Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at a low substrate concentration, indicating HIGH affinity (the enzyme binds and processes substrate effectively even when substrate is scarce); a HIGH Km indicates lower affinity (more substrate is needed to achieve the same fractional saturation). Vmax reflects the maximum catalytic capacity of the enzyme population under the given conditions, once the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate — it depends on the total amount/concentration of enzyme present and each enzyme molecule's intrinsic turnover number (kcat, how quickly an individual enzyme molecule converts bound substrate to product).

(b)(i) Inhibitor A: Vmax unchanged (50, same as no inhibitor) but Km increased (120 vs. 40) → classified as a COMPETITIVE inhibitor. A higher apparent Km means more substrate is required to reach half-maximal velocity, consistent with the inhibitor competing with substrate for the same binding site — but because sufficiently high substrate concentration can still outcompete the inhibitor, the same Vmax can eventually be reached.
Inhibitor B: Vmax decreased (25 vs. 50) but Km unchanged (40, same as no inhibitor) → classified as a NONCOMPETITIVE inhibitor. Vmax is reduced because a fraction of enzyme molecules is rendered nonfunctional regardless of substrate concentration, but the affinity (Km) of the remaining active enzyme for substrate is unaffected, since this inhibitor does not compete at the active site.

(b)(ii) Competitive inhibitor (A): binds reversibly to the enzyme's active site itself, typically because it structurally resembles the substrate, physically blocking the substrate from binding there. Because this competition is reversible and concentration-dependent, sufficiently high substrate concentrations can outcompete/displace the inhibitor from the active site, so the reaction can still eventually reach the same Vmax as uninhibited enzyme (just requiring more substrate — a higher apparent Km).
Noncompetitive inhibitor (B): binds to a site on the enzyme distinct from the active site (an allosteric site), inducing a conformational change that impairs or abolishes the enzyme's catalytic activity regardless of how much substrate is bound. Because it does not compete with substrate for the active site, increasing substrate concentration cannot reverse this inhibition — the Vmax of the enzyme population is reduced (some fraction of enzyme is nonfunctional at any time), while the Km (affinity) of the still-active, uninhibited enzyme molecules remains unchanged.

(c) Threonine deaminase catalyzes the first committed step of the pathway converting threonine to isoleucine. Isoleucine, the pathway's end product, binds threonine deaminase at an allosteric site — a regulatory binding site physically and structurally distinct from the active site, where threonine itself binds and is chemically converted. When isoleucine binds this allosteric site, it induces a conformational change that is transmitted through the enzyme's tertiary/quaternary structure to the active site, distorting its shape so that it can no longer efficiently bind threonine or catalyze the reaction — reducing enzyme activity. This is feedback inhibition (end-product inhibition): the pathway's own final product inhibits an enzyme earlier in its own biosynthetic pathway, creating a self-regulating mechanism — as isoleucine accumulates to sufficient levels, it shuts down further isoleucine production by inhibiting threonine deaminase, preventing wasteful overproduction; as isoleucine is consumed/depleted, inhibition is relieved and the pathway resumes.

(d)(i) From 0°C up to the temperature optimum, increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of enzyme and substrate molecules, increasing both the frequency and the energy of molecular collisions between them; this increases the rate at which enzyme–substrate complexes form and successfully proceed to products, so reaction rate increases with temperature in this range.
(d)(ii) Above the temperature optimum, reaction rate decreases sharply because excess thermal energy disrupts the weak, noncovalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that maintain the enzyme's precise tertiary/quaternary structure. The enzyme begins to denature (unfold from its native, catalytically functional conformation), progressively distorting or destroying the specific shape of the active site required for substrate binding and catalysis, so catalytic activity falls off rapidly as an increasing fraction of enzyme molecules become permanently denatured and nonfunctional.
(d)(iii) A thermophilic bacterium's enzyme would likely have structural features that create MORE and/or stronger stabilizing interactions holding its tertiary/quaternary structure together — e.g., more ionic bonds/salt bridges, more hydrogen bonds, more disulfide bonds, and/or tighter hydrophobic core packing — than the equivalent mesophilic enzyme. These additional stabilizing interactions allow the thermophilic protein to resist thermal denaturation and maintain its functional 3D conformation (and active-site shape) at the higher temperatures characteristic of the thermophile's environment, whereas the mesophilic enzyme's comparatively fewer/weaker stabilizing interactions cause it to denature at the lower temperatures typical of mesophilic environments.

(d)(i) From 0°C up to the temperature optimum, increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of enzyme and substrate molecules, increasing both the frequency and the energy of molecular collisions between them; this increases the rate at which enzyme–substrate complexes form and successfully proceed to products, so reaction rate increases with temperature in this range.
(d)(ii) Above the temperature optimum, reaction rate decreases sharply because excess thermal energy disrupts the weak, noncovalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that maintain the enzyme's precise tertiary/quaternary structure. The enzyme begins to denature (unfold from its native, catalytically functional conformation), progressively distorting or destroying the specific shape of the active site required for substrate binding and catalysis, so catalytic activity falls off rapidly as an increasing fraction of enzyme molecules become permanently denatured and nonfunctional.
(d)(iii) A thermophilic bacterium's enzyme would likely have structural features that create MORE and/or stronger stabilizing interactions holding its tertiary/quaternary structure together — e.g., more ionic bonds/salt bridges, more hydrogen bonds, more disulfide bonds, and/or tighter hydrophobic core packing — than the equivalent mesophilic enzyme. These additional stabilizing interactions allow the thermophilic protein to resist thermal denaturation and maintain its functional 3D conformation (and active-site shape) at the higher temperatures characteristic of the thermophile's environment, whereas the mesophilic enzyme's comparatively fewer/weaker stabilizing interactions cause it to denature at the lower temperatures typical of mesophilic environments.

full_text:
(a) mRNA encoding trypsinogen is translated by ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): a signal sequence on the growing polypeptide is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP), directing the ribosome to dock at the RER membrane, and the polypeptide is threaded into the RER lumen as it is synthesized, where it begins folding (assisted by chaperone proteins) and is glycosylated. The protein is then packaged into COPII-coated transport vesicles that bud from the RER membrane and travel to and fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus, releasing their contents into the Golgi lumen. Within the Golgi, the protein is further modified (glycosylation patterns altered, proteolytic processing) as it moves from the cis face through the medial cisternae toward the trans face, transported between Golgi cisternae. At the trans face, the mature trypsinogen is packaged into secretory vesicles, which bud off and travel to the plasma membrane, fusing with it (exocytosis) to release trypsinogen out of the pancreatic acinar cell into the pancreatic duct.

(b) Three functions of the smooth ER (SER) in a liver cell: (1) Detoxification of drugs and other lipid-soluble toxins — SER membranes contain enzymes (e.g., cytochrome P450 family enzymes) that chemically modify (e.g., hydroxylate) hydrophobic toxic compounds and drugs, increasing their water solubility so they can be excreted from the body. (2) Lipid and steroid synthesis — SER synthesizes membrane phospholipids, cholesterol, and (in steroid-hormone-producing cells) steroid hormones, as well as lipoprotein components. (3) Carbohydrate/glucose metabolism — SER contains the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase, which removes the phosphate group from glucose-6-phosphate (generated by glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis), producing free glucose that can be transported out of the liver cell into the bloodstream to help regulate blood glucose levels (glucose-6-phosphate itself cannot cross the plasma membrane).
Molecular basis of detoxification: cytochrome P450 enzymes embedded in the SER membrane catalyze oxidation reactions (e.g., adding a hydroxyl group) to hydrophobic drug/toxin molecules, increasing their polarity and water solubility; this allows subsequent conjugation (e.g., with glucuronic acid) and excretion via bile or urine, preventing the accumulation of these lipid-soluble compounds within cell membranes.

(c)(i) Lysosomal (acid hydrolase) enzymes synthesized in the RER are tagged in the Golgi apparatus with a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) marker. Mannose-6-phosphate receptors located in the trans-Golgi network specifically recognize and bind M6P-tagged proteins, sorting them into clathrin-coated vesicles that are directed to lysosomes (or late endosomes that mature into lysosomes), rather than following the default pathway toward the plasma membrane for secretion — this specific tag-and-receptor recognition system targets lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes instead of being secreted out of the cell.

(c)(ii) Lysosomal acid hydrolases require the low (acidic, ~pH 5) internal pH of the lysosome (maintained by proton pumps in the lysosomal membrane) to be catalytically active; at the neutral pH of the cytosol, these enzymes are far less active, so even minor leakage into the cytosol would not significantly damage other cell components. Additionally, proteins on the inner (lumen-facing) surface of the lysosomal membrane are highly glycosylated, which helps shield/protect them from being degraded by the very enzymes contained within the lysosome.

(c)(iii) When a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome (a double-membrane vesicle that has engulfed damaged organelles or cytoplasmic material for recycling), it forms an autolysosome. The lysosome's acid hydrolases mix with and enzymatically digest the enclosed material — proteins, lipids, and damaged organelle components — breaking them down into their monomer building blocks (amino acids, fatty acids, sugars, nucleotides). These monomers are then transported out of the (auto)lysosome back into the cytosol, where the cell can recycle/reuse them for new biosynthesis or as an energy source.

(d) Brefeldin A disrupts COPI vesicle formation and causes the Golgi apparatus to collapse back into the ER.
(i) Secretion of a newly synthesized extracellular protein: would be blocked/severely decreased. With the Golgi structurally collapsed into the ER and normal ER→Golgi→plasma membrane vesicular traffic disrupted, the protein cannot be properly processed and packaged into secretory vesicles for exocytosis, so secretion out of the cell would stop or drop sharply.
(ii) Delivery of lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes: also blocked/severely impaired, because the trans-Golgi network (where lysosomal enzymes are normally M6P-tagged and sorted into lysosome-directed vesicles) is disrupted along with the rest of the Golgi — without a functional Golgi to apply this tag and sort the enzymes, they cannot be properly targeted to lysosomes.
(iii) ER morphology: the ER would appear enlarged/swollen and structurally abnormal, since Golgi membrane and its resident/cargo proteins are being redistributed back into (fused with) the ER, increasing the ER's membrane surface area and volume and altering its normal appearance — this collapse is the basis for using brefeldin A experimentally to study ER–Golgi trafficking.

full_text:
(a)(i) Four lines of evidence for the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria: (1) Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA genome (mtDNA), structurally similar to bacterial chromosomes (circular, not complexed with histones), distinct from the linear, histone-associated nuclear DNA of the eukaryotic host. (2) Mitochondria contain their own ribosomes, which resemble bacterial (70S-type) ribosomes in size and antibiotic sensitivity, rather than the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic host cell. (3) Mitochondria are bounded by a double membrane: the inner membrane is thought to derive from the original engulfed bacterium's own plasma membrane, while the outer membrane is thought to derive from the host cell's plasma membrane/engulfing vesicle formed during the initial phagocytic/endocytic event. (4) Mitochondria reproduce independently of the host cell cycle via binary fission, similar to how free-living bacteria divide, rather than being newly assembled by the cell each time. (Additional supporting evidence: phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial rRNA/protein sequences shows mitochondria are most closely related to a specific group of alpha-proteobacteria.)

(a)(ii) Over evolutionary time, most genes originally present in the free-living bacterial ancestor's genome were transferred from the mitochondrial genome to the host cell's nuclear genome (endosymbiotic/organellar gene transfer); the corresponding proteins are now synthesized in the cytosol by cytoplasmic ribosomes and imported back into the mitochondrion via specific protein-targeting signal sequences. Retaining most genes in the nucleus is advantageous because it allows the cell to centrally coordinate/regulate mitochondrial protein production together with the rest of the cell's needs, benefits from the nucleus's more robust and accurate DNA repair/recombination machinery (mitochondrial DNA has a higher mutation rate and less effective repair), and reduces genomic redundancy — the mitochondrial genome now retains only a small number of genes, typically those encoding highly hydrophobic membrane proteins (e.g., core electron transport chain subunits) that are difficult to import from the cytosol after synthesis.

(b) The source of the proton gradient is the electron transport chain: as electrons from NADH (and FADH2) are passed sequentially through Complexes I, III, and IV, the energy released by these electron transfers is used by each complex to actively pump H+ ions from the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, creating a higher H+ concentration (and more positive charge/lower pH) in the intermembrane space than in the matrix — an electrochemical proton gradient (proton-motive force). This gradient drives ATP synthesis via chemiosmosis: because the inner membrane is impermeable to ions except through specific channels, H+ can flow back down its concentration gradient (from intermembrane space into the matrix) only through the F0 channel of ATP synthase; this proton flow spins the F0 rotor, driving conformational changes in the F1 head that catalyze phosphorylation of ADP + Pi to form ATP.
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): oxidizes NADH back to NAD+, passing the released electrons into the electron transport chain, and pumps 4 H+ into the intermembrane space.
Complex III (cytochrome bc1): continues passing electrons along the chain and pumps 4 H+ into the intermembrane space.
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): accepts electrons from cytochrome c and transfers them to the final electron acceptor, O2, reducing it (with H+ from the matrix) to H2O, and pumps 2 additional H+ into the intermembrane space.
ATP synthase (Complex V): uses the energy of protons flowing back through its F0 channel down the electrochemical gradient to drive the rotary catalytic mechanism of its F1 head, synthesizing ATP from ADP and Pi.

(c)(i) Rotenone (inhibits Complex I): electrons from NADH can no longer enter the electron transport chain at Complex I, blocking electron flow through the chain from that entry point. O2 consumption DECREASES (electrons can no longer reach Complex IV via this pathway at the normal rate), and ATP synthesis DECREASES correspondingly (the proton gradient can no longer be adequately maintained, reducing ATP synthase activity).

(c)(ii) Oligomycin (blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase): protons can no longer flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, so ATP synthesis DECREASES/stops directly. Because the proton gradient can no longer be dissipated through ATP synthase, H+ accumulates in the intermembrane space, increasing the gradient's magnitude/"back pressure" against further proton pumping; this makes continued pumping by the ETC complexes energetically less favorable, so electron transport (and thus O2 consumption) also DECREASES — both O2 consumption and ATP synthesis decrease.

(c)(iii) DNP (uncoupler; makes the inner membrane permeable to H+): protons leak directly back into the matrix across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase entirely, so the proton gradient cannot build up (it is continuously dissipated as heat rather than being used to synthesize ATP) — ATP synthesis DECREASES, since protons no longer need to flow through ATP synthase to return to the matrix. However, because the gradient never builds up significant "back pressure," the ETC complexes can pump protons essentially unimpeded, and the cell/mitochondrion compensates for the lost ATP output by increasing the rate of electron transport — so O2 consumption INCREASES, even though little of that respiratory energy is captured as ATP (most is released as heat).

(d) Heart muscle cells and neurons both have unusually high ATP demands: cardiac muscle cells must contract continuously throughout life to pump blood, requiring constant ATP for the actin–myosin contractile machinery, and neurons require large amounts of ATP to maintain ion gradients (via the Na+/K+ ATPase) for generating and propagating action potentials and for synaptic transmission (neurotransmitter synthesis, vesicle trafficking/recycling) — both cell types are highly metabolically active and depend heavily on the efficient, high-ATP-yield process of oxidative phosphorylation. (3) Mitochondria are bounded by a double membrane: the inner membrane is thought to derive from the original engulfed bacterium's own plasma membrane, while the outer membrane is thought to derive from the host cell's plasma membrane/engulfing vesicle formed during the initial phagocytic/endocytic event. (4) Mitochondria reproduce independently of the host cell cycle via binary fission, similar to how free-living bacteria divide, rather than being newly assembled by the cell each time. (Additional supporting evidence: phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial rRNA/protein sequences shows mitochondria are most closely related to a specific group of alpha-proteobacteria.)

(a)(ii) Over evolutionary time, most genes originally present in the free-living bacterial ancestor's genome were transferred from the mitochondrial genome to the host cell's nuclear genome (endosymbiotic/organellar gene transfer); the corresponding proteins are now synthesized in the cytosol by cytoplasmic ribosomes and imported back into the mitochondrion via specific protein-targeting signal sequences. Retaining most genes in the nucleus is advantageous because it allows the cell to centrally coordinate/regulate mitochondrial protein production together with the rest of the cell's needs, benefits from the nucleus's more robust and accurate DNA repair/recombination machinery (mitochondrial DNA has a higher mutation rate and less effective repair), and reduces genomic redundancy — the mitochondrial genome now retains only a small number of genes, typically those encoding highly hydrophobic membrane proteins (e.g., core electron transport chain subunits) that are difficult to import from the cytosol after synthesis.

ATP synthase (Complex V): uses the energy of protons flowing back through its F0 channel down the electrochemical gradient to drive the rotary catalytic mechanism of its F1 head, synthesizing ATP from ADP and Pi.

full_text:
(a) Carbon trace: Glycolysis splits glucose (6C) into 2 pyruvate (3C each); no carbon is lost as CO2 in glycolysis, so all 6 carbons remain in the 2 pyruvate molecules. In pyruvate oxidation, each pyruvate (3C) is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA (2C) plus 1 CO2, releasing 2 CO2 total (one per pyruvate) and leaving 4 carbons in the two acetyl groups. In the Krebs cycle, each acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate; over one turn, 2 CO2 are released via two decarboxylation steps (isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase). Since the cycle turns twice (once per acetyl-CoA), 4 CO2 are released total. Overall CO2 accounting: 2 CO2 (pyruvate oxidation) + 4 CO2 (Krebs, 2 turns) = 6 CO2, accounting for all 6 original glucose carbons.

(b) Electron carriers produced per glucose: Glycolysis produces 2 NADH (cytoplasmic). Pyruvate oxidation produces 2 NADH (mitochondrial matrix, one per pyruvate). The Krebs cycle (2 turns) produces 6 NADH and 2 FADH2. Total = 10 NADH (2 cytoplasmic + 8 mitochondrial) and 2 FADH2. Mitochondrial NADH donates its electrons to Complex I of the electron transport chain, pumping protons at Complexes I, III, and IV (~2.5 ATP equivalent each). FADH2 donates electrons to Complex II, bypassing Complex I, so it only drives proton pumping at Complexes III and IV (~1.5 ATP equivalent each). The 2 cytoplasmic NADH from glycolysis cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly and must be shuttled in via the malate-aspartate shuttle (delivers electrons to mitochondrial NAD+, yielding the full ~2.5 ATP equivalent) or the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (delivers electrons to FAD, yielding only ~1.5 ATP equivalent).

(c) Three reasons actual ATP yield is lower than the theoretical ~30-32 ATP: (1) Proton leak — some protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane through channels other than ATP synthase, dissipating part of the proton-motive force as heat rather than using it to synthesize ATP. (2) Shuttle costs — cytoplasmic NADH shuttled via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers electrons to FAD instead of NAD+, losing about 1 ATP equivalent per cytoplasmic NADH compared to the theoretical maximum that assumes full NADH-level input. (3) The proton gradient is used for purposes other than ATP synthesis, such as powering the transport of ADP into and ATP out of the mitochondrial matrix (via the adenine nucleotide translocase) and importing inorganic phosphate and pyruvate, which consumes some of the gradient's energy without directly producing ATP.

(d) The Pasteur effect: without O2, there is no terminal electron acceptor for the electron transport chain, so oxidative phosphorylation stops and NADH cannot be reoxidized to NAD+ via the ETC. Glycolysis absolutely requires a continuous supply of NAD+ (used by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase); under anaerobic conditions this NAD+ is regenerated instead by fermentation (reducing pyruvate to lactate or acetaldehyde to ethanol), which allows glycolysis to keep running. However, anaerobic glycolysis alone nets only 2 ATP per glucose via substrate-level phosphorylation, versus ~30 ATP aerobically — roughly a 15-fold drop in efficiency. To meet the same cellular energy demand, the cell must dramatically increase glycolytic flux, consistent with Table 1 showing glucose consumption jumping from 0.5 to 4.2 mmol/hr/g (about 8x) under anaerobic conditions. This increase is driven by regulation of phosphofructokinase (PFK), the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme: ATP and citrate (both more abundant when the Krebs cycle/ETC are active) are allosteric inhibitors of PFK, while AMP and ADP (more abundant when ATP production falls under anaerobic conditions) are allosteric activators. Anaerobically, falling ATP/citrate and rising AMP/ADP relieve PFK inhibition and activate it, ramping up glycolytic rate to compensate for the far lower ATP yield per glucose molecule.

derivations.expression: (c) Three reasons actual ATP yield is lower than the theoretical ~30-32 ATP: (1) Proton leak — some protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane through channels other than ATP synthase, dissipating part of the proton-motive force as heat rather than using it to synthesize ATP. (2) Shuttle costs — cytoplasmic NADH shuttled via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers electrons to FAD instead of NAD+, losing about 1 ATP equivalent per cytoplasmic NADH compared to the theoretical maximum that assumes full NADH-level input. (3) The proton gradient is used for purposes other than ATP synthesis, such as powering the transport of ADP into and ATP out of the mitochondrial matrix (via the adenine nucleotide translocase) and importing inorganic phosphate and pyruvate, which consumes some of the gradient's energy without directly producing ATP.

derivations.expression: (d) The Pasteur effect: without O2, there is no terminal electron acceptor for the electron transport chain, so oxidative phosphorylation stops and NADH cannot be reoxidized to NAD+ via the ETC. Glycolysis absolutely requires a continuous supply of NAD+ (used by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase); under anaerobic conditions this NAD+ is regenerated instead by fermentation (reducing pyruvate to lactate or acetaldehyde to ethanol), which allows glycolysis to keep running. However, anaerobic glycolysis alone nets only 2 ATP per glucose via substrate-level phosphorylation, versus ~30 ATP aerobically — roughly a 15-fold drop in efficiency. To meet the same cellular energy demand, the cell must dramatically increase glycolytic flux, consistent with Table 1 showing glucose consumption jumping from 0.5 to 4.2 mmol/hr/g (about 8x) under anaerobic conditions. This increase is driven by regulation of phosphofructokinase (PFK), the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme: ATP and citrate (both more abundant when the Krebs cycle/ETC are active) are allosteric inhibitors of PFK, while AMP and ADP (more abundant when ATP production falls under anaerobic conditions) are allosteric activators. Anaerobically, falling ATP/citrate and rising AMP/ADP relieve PFK inhibition and activate it, ramping up glycolytic rate to compensate for the far lower ATP yield per glucose molecule.

full_text:
(a) Alcoholic fermentation (yeast): Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation) and 2 NADH. Pyruvate decarboxylase removes a carboxyl group from each pyruvate, releasing CO2 and forming acetaldehyde. Alcohol dehydrogenase then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ in the process. Net reaction: glucose to 2 ethanol + 2 CO2. Lactic acid fermentation (exercising muscle): glycolysis proceeds identically (2 ATP, 2 NADH). Lactate dehydrogenase directly reduces pyruvate to lactate, oxidizing NADH to NAD+; no CO2 is released. In both pathways, the enzyme catalyzing the final, defining step is lactate dehydrogenase (muscle) or alcohol dehydrogenase (yeast), and the metabolic purpose in both cases is identical: regenerate NAD+ so that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in glycolysis can keep functioning, allowing glycolysis (the only ATP-producing step available without O2) to continue.

(b) The claim is false/misleading. full_text:
(a) Insulin binds the alpha-subunits of the insulin receptor, causing a conformational change that activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the beta-subunits; the beta-subunits trans-autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. These phosphotyrosines serve as docking sites that recruit and phosphorylate IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1). Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits PI3K via SH2 domains; PI3K phosphorylates membrane PIP2 to PIP3. PIP3 recruits both PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the plasma membrane, where PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. Active Akt phosphorylates AS160, inhibiting its normal suppression of Rab GTPases; this permits GLUT4-containing vesicles to translocate to and fuse with the plasma membrane, inserting GLUT4 glucose transporters and enabling glucose uptake.

(b) Insulin/RTK pathway: receptor type is a single-pass transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase located on the cell surface; the primary second messenger/amplifier is the PI3K to PIP3 to Akt phosphorylation cascade; physiological effect includes GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake (also glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis via mTOR). Epinephrine/GPCR (beta-adrenergic) pathway: receptor type is a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface, coupled to a Gs protein; the second messenger is cyclic AMP (cAMP), produced by adenylyl cyclase and activating protein kinase A (PKA); physiological effect includes glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) in liver/muscle via PKA-mediated activation of glycogen phosphorylase kinase, raising blood glucose as part of the fight-or-flight response.

(c) Three consequences of a constitutively active insulin receptor: (1) Metabolic effects — continuous Akt activation drives ongoing GLUT4 translocation and glycogen synthase activation (via GSK-3 inhibition), causing excessive, insulin-independent glucose uptake and storage, risking hypoglycemia and disrupted glucose homeostasis. (2) Cell proliferation — sustained activation of Akt/mTOR (and likely the parallel Ras/MAPK branch downstream of the RTK) promotes continuous protein synthesis and cell growth signals, potentially driving uncontrolled proliferation. (3) Gene expression effects — continuous phosphorylation and inactivation of FOXO transcription factors (which normally activate genes for gluconeogenesis and stress response/apoptosis when unphosphorylated) suppresses these FOXO target genes, altering glucose production pathways and reducing normal apoptotic/stress responses, which could favor unchecked cell survival.

(d)(i) HER2 overexpression: more receptor molecules on the cell surface increases the likelihood of ligand-independent receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, chronically activating downstream growth pathways (Ras/MAPK, PI3K/Akt) even without normal levels of growth factor, driving continuous proliferation signaling.
(ii) Ras locked in GTP-bound form: Ras normally functions as a molecular switch, active when GTP-bound and inactivated when it hydrolyzes GTP to GDP (assisted by GAPs); a mutation that prevents GTP hydrolysis leaves Ras permanently active, continuously stimulating the MAPK/ERK cascade and driving persistent proliferation signals to the nucleus regardless of upstream receptor activation.
(iii) PTEN loss-of-function: PTEN normally converts PIP3 back to PIP2, acting as a brake on the PI3K/Akt pathway; without functional PTEN, PIP3 accumulates unchecked, causing constitutive Akt activation and continuous pro-growth, pro-survival, anti-apoptotic signaling that drives uncontrolled proliferation and resistance to programmed cell death.

Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits PI3K via SH2 domains; PI3K phosphorylates membrane PIP2 to PIP3. PIP3 recruits both PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the plasma membrane, where PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. Active Akt phosphorylates AS160, inhibiting its normal suppression of Rab GTPases; this permits GLUT4-containing vesicles to translocate to and fuse with the plasma membrane, inserting GLUT4 glucose transporters and enabling glucose uptake.

derivations.expression: (c) Three consequences of a constitutively active insulin receptor: (1) Metabolic effects — continuous Akt activation drives ongoing GLUT4 translocation and glycogen synthase activation (via GSK-3 inhibition), causing excessive, insulin-independent glucose uptake and storage, risking hypoglycemia and disrupted glucose homeostasis. (2) Cell proliferation — sustained activation of Akt/mTOR (and likely the parallel Ras/MAPK branch downstream of the RTK) promotes continuous protein synthesis and cell growth signals, potentially driving uncontrolled proliferation. (3) Gene expression effects — continuous phosphorylation and inactivation of FOXO transcription factors (which normally activate genes for gluconeogenesis and stress response/apoptosis when unphosphorylated) suppresses these FOXO target genes, altering glucose production pathways and reducing normal apoptotic/stress responses, which could favor unchecked cell survival.

(d)(i) HER2 overexpression: more receptor molecules on the cell surface increases the likelihood of ligand-independent receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, chronically activating downstream growth pathways (Ras/MAPK, PI3K/Akt) even without normal levels of growth factor, driving continuous proliferation signaling.
(ii) Ras locked in GTP-bound form: Ras normally functions as a molecular switch, active when GTP-bound and inactivated when it hydrolyzes GTP to GDP (assisted by GAPs); a mutation that prevents GTP hydrolysis leaves Ras permanently active, continuously stimulating the MAPK/ERK cascade and driving persistent proliferation signals to the nucleus regardless of upstream receptor activation.
(iii) PTEN loss-of-function: PTEN normally converts PIP3 back to PIP2, acting as a brake on the PI3K/Akt pathway; without functional PTEN, PIP3 accumulates unchecked, causing constitutive Akt activation and continuous pro-growth, pro-survival, anti-apoptotic signaling that drives uncontrolled proliferation and resistance to programmed cell death.

full_text:
(a)(i) Most likely mode of inheritance: X-linked recessive. Two supporting pedigree observations: (1) only males are affected (no affected females appear anywhere in the pedigree), consistent with a recessive allele on the X chromosome where males need only one copy (hemizygous) to be affected while females need two copies; (2) the trait appears to skip a generation through an unaffected carrier female (II-4, unaffected, yet has an affected son III-1), which is the classic X-linked recessive pattern of transmission through unaffected carrier mothers rather than direct parent-to-offspring transmission in every generation.
(ii) Genotypes: I-1 = X^A Y (unaffected male); I-2 = X^A X^a (obligate carrier, since she must have transmitted the recessive allele that appears in affected descendants); II-3 = X^a Y (affected male); II-4 = X^A X^a (unaffected carrier female, confirmed by having an affected son).
(iii) Cross II-4 (X^A X^a, carrier female) x II-3 (X^a Y, affected male) gives offspring: 1/4 X^A X^a (carrier female), 1/4 X^a X^a (affected female), 1/4 X^A Y (unaffected male), 1/4 X^a Y (affected male). The probability of an affected female (X^a X^a) is 1/4 (25%): the affected father II-3 always contributes X^a to every daughter, and the carrier mother II-4 contributes X^a to half of her offspring, so a daughter is affected only if she also receives X^a from her mother -- 1/2 (mother's X^a) x 1 (father's obligate X^a) = 1/4.

(b) Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes -- they have only a single X chromosome (paired with a Y chromosome that lacks a homologous allele for most X-linked genes), so a single copy of a recessive allele is sufficient to produce the affected phenotype in males, with no second allele to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes, so a single recessive allele is typically masked by a normal dominant allele on the other X chromosome (heterozygous carrier females are unaffected); females must inherit the recessive allele from both parents to be affected, which is much less likely, especially for rare alleles, explaining the much higher frequency of affected males.

(c)(i) X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development, around the blastocyst stage (approximately day 5-6 in humans), independently in each cell of the female embryo. The choice of which X chromosome (maternal or paternal) is inactivated in each cell is random.
(ii) The Xist gene, located on the X chromosome destined to be inactivated, is upregulated and transcribes a long non-coding RNA (Xist RNA) that coats that X chromosome in cis; this recruits chromatin-modifying complexes that establish heterochromatin (histone deacetylation and methylation, DNA methylation), condensing that chromosome into a transcriptionally silent Barr body.
(iii) X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited because once a given cell inactivates a specific X chromosome, the epigenetic marks (including DNA methylation patterns) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and passed on to all of that cell's mitotic descendants, so each clonal lineage of cells maintains the same inactivated X, producing stable patches of tissue expressing only one parental X allele.

(d)(i) Tortoiseshell cats are almost always female because the orange/black coat color gene is X-linked; a heterozygous female undergoes random X-inactivation, creating two populations of cells -- some expressing the orange allele, others the black allele -- producing a patched, two-color coat. Males are hemizygous (XY) and carry only one allele, so they are uniformly either orange or black (except in rare XXY males).
(ii) The patches are large rather than finely blended because X-inactivation happens early in development when the embryo consists of relatively few cells; each of those early cells' clonal descendants (forming a large contiguous patch of tissue) all inherit the same inactivated X, so entire regions of skin trace back to a single early progenitor with one particular X active, producing large, blocky patches rather than a fine intermixed pattern.
(iii) A female homozygous for the orange allele would be entirely orange, with no black patches, because every cell expresses the orange allele regardless of which X chromosome is inactivated.

(c)(i) X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development, around the blastocyst stage (approximately day 5-6 in humans), independently in each cell of the female embryo. The choice of which X chromosome (maternal or paternal) is inactivated in each cell is random.
(ii) The Xist gene, located on the X chromosome destined to be inactivated, is upregulated and transcribes a long non-coding RNA (Xist RNA) that coats that X chromosome in cis; this recruits chromatin-modifying complexes that establish heterochromatin (histone deacetylation and methylation, DNA methylation), condensing that chromosome into a transcriptionally silent Barr body.
(iii) X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited because once a given cell inactivates a specific X chromosome, the epigenetic marks (including DNA methylation patterns) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and passed on to all of that cell's mitotic descendants, so each clonal lineage of cells maintains the same inactivated X, producing stable patches of tissue expressing only one parental X allele.

full_text:
(a)(i) Pre-initiation complex (PIC) assembly: TFIID (via its TBP subunit) binds the TATA box in the promoter and bends the DNA, nucleating assembly of the complex; this recruits TFIIA and TFIIB, which stabilize TFIID binding and help correctly position RNA Polymerase II at the transcription start site. RNA Pol II is recruited together with TFIIF; TFIIE and TFIIH then join the complex. TFIIH has both helicase activity (unwinds the DNA at the start site, forming the transcription bubble) and kinase activity (phosphorylates the C-terminal domain, CTD, of RNA Pol II), which triggers promoter escape and the start of transcription. Two general transcription factors and their roles: TFIID (binds the TATA box via TBP, nucleates PIC assembly) and TFIIH (unwinds promoter DNA and phosphorylates the Pol II CTD to initiate transcription).
(ii) Enhancers act at a distance through DNA looping: activator proteins bind the enhancer sequence; the Mediator complex physically bridges these DNA-bound activators with the general transcription machinery (including RNA Pol II and the general transcription factors) assembled at the promoter, causing the intervening DNA to loop out so the enhancer and promoter come into close physical proximity despite being far apart in linear sequence. This interaction stabilizes PIC assembly at the promoter and increases the rate of transcription initiation.

(b)(i) Euchromatin has hyperacetylated histones, is loosely packed in a "beads-on-a-string" (10 nm fiber) conformation with accessible DNA. Heterochromatin has hypoacetylated (deacetylated) and often methylated histones (for example, H3K9 trimethylation), and is tightly compacted (30 nm+ fiber), rendering the DNA inaccessible.
(ii) Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) add acetyl groups to lysine residues on histone tails, neutralizing their positive charge; this weakens the electrostatic attraction between the histones and the negatively charged DNA backbone, loosening chromatin structure and increasing accessibility for transcription factors and RNA polymerase, thereby activating transcription. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove these acetyl groups, restoring the positive charge on histones, tightening histone-DNA interactions, condensing chromatin, and repressing transcription.
(iii) Trichostatin A inhibits HDACs, causing acetyl groups to accumulate on histones (global hyperacetylation). Chromatin becomes more open and accessible throughout the genome, which generally increases global gene expression, since more promoters and regulatory regions become accessible to transcription factors and RNA polymerase.

(c)(i) The DNA-binding domain alone produces only baseline expression (about 1), demonstrating that binding to the promoter DNA is necessary but not sufficient to activate transcription — the DBD can locate and occupy the target sequence but cannot itself recruit the machinery needed to activate transcription without an activation domain.
(ii) The different activation domains produce very different levels of activation (45, 12, 87), showing that activation is modular and that activation domains vary substantially in their ability to recruit and stimulate the transcriptional machinery, likely reflecting differences in the specific protein-protein interactions each domain can make with coactivators, chromatin remodelers, or Mediator. The combined AD1 + AD3 result (203) exceeding either domain alone demonstrates a synergistic (more than additive) effect when multiple activation domains act together.
(iii) Because Activation Domain 3 physically interacts with the Mediator complex, it can directly recruit Mediator to the promoter region; Mediator in turn helps recruit and stabilize RNA Polymerase II and the general transcription factors at the promoter, increasing the efficiency of PIC assembly and the rate of transcription initiation, explaining AD3's strong activation of gene expression (87 relative units).

(d)(i) Combinatorial control: different cell types express different combinations of transcription factors. A given gene's regulatory elements often require a specific combination of multiple transcription factors bound simultaneously to be activated, so the gene is only expressed in cell types that happen to express that particular combination of factors; this allows a relatively limited number of transcription factors to generate many distinct, cell-type-specific gene expression patterns combinatorially.
(ii) Epigenetic inheritance: the chromatin state (DNA methylation patterns and histone modifications) established at specific genes during differentiation is stably maintained and copied through successive rounds of DNA replication and mitosis, so a differentiated cell's daughter cells retain the same pattern of active and silenced genes as the parent cell — this preserves cell-type identity across many cell divisions without requiring the pattern of gene expression to be re-established from scratch in every generation of cells.

full_text:
(a)(i) A bottleneck is a sudden, drastic reduction in population size that leaves only a small, random subset of the original gene pool; which alleles survive is a matter of chance, unrelated to their fitness effects, so rare alleles are often lost regardless of whether they were helpful, harmful, or neutral. Natural selection instead changes allele frequencies in a consistent, fitness-driven direction: alleles that improve survival/reproduction become more common and alleles that reduce fitness become less common. A bottleneck reduces diversity non-directionally; selection changes frequencies directionally based on adaptive value.
(a)(ii) That cheetahs can accept skin grafts from virtually any unrelated cheetah shows they are genetically extremely similar to one another -- the self-recognition proteins on their cells are nearly identical across the population, so the immune system does not detect transplanted tissue as foreign. This is the signature of a population that lost most of its genetic variation in a severe bottleneck; a genetically diverse population would reject grafts between unrelated individuals.
(a)(iii) Genetic diversity is set by how many different alleles were present among the individuals who actually contributed offspring, which for the elephant seals was capped at roughly 20 survivors during the bottleneck. Regaining numbers afterward does not add back alleles that were already lost -- diversity can only be recovered slowly, through new mutation accumulating over many generations, not simply by the population growing larger. The modern population, despite its size, still carries only the reduced genetic variation of the ~20 individuals that founded its recovery.

(b)(i) Inbreeding increases the chance that an offspring inherits two identical copies of the same allele (one from each related parent), raising homozygosity across the genome. Most seriously harmful alleles are recessive and normally masked in heterozygotes; increased homozygosity exposes these recessive deleterious alleles in the phenotype, lowering fitness (survival, fertility) -- this is inbreeding depression.
(b)(ii) Population B has much lower mean heterozygosity (0.01 vs. 0.04) and lower allelic richness (1.8 vs. 3.2 alleles/locus) than Population A, along with far higher rates of kinked tails (85% vs. 50%) and cryptic testes (90% vs. 55%). This pattern indicates Population B has undergone substantially more inbreeding. Predicted consequences: reduced male fertility (cryptic testes impair sperm production), possible impaired mobility from the tail defect, and lower overall reproductive success and offspring survival -- the expected signs of inbreeding depression.

(c)(i) Genetic rescue works by breeding in unrelated individuals carrying different alleles than the inbred population. Offspring of these crosses are heterozygous at many loci where residents were homozygous, so functional alleles from the immigrants mask the residents' harmful recessive alleles, producing a fitness increase (heterosis/hybrid vigor) that offsets inbreeding depression.
(c)(ii) Two risks: (1) Outbreeding depression -- the introduced subspecies may carry alleles or trait combinations adapted to a different environment, so hybrid offspring may be less well-suited to Florida conditions than pure-bred residents. (2) Loss of local genetic distinctiveness ("genetic swamping") -- if introduced alleles spread widely, the unique genetic identity of the original Florida subspecies could be diluted or lost.
(c)(iii) Hybrid (puma x panther) offspring should show higher heterozygosity and higher cub survival than pure panther offspring, because the puma parent's alleles mask homozygous deleterious recessive alleles inherited from the inbred panther lineage (heterosis). This matches the historical data: cub survival rose from 20% to 50% after the 1995 introduction.

(d)(i) Genetic diversity is the raw material selection needs to respond to change: when a new pathogen or environmental shift occurs, a genetically diverse population is more likely to already contain individuals whose alleles happen to confer resistance or tolerance, allowing selection to increase those alleles' frequency so the population adapts. A population with very low genetic diversity has few alternative alleles available, so if the existing alleles are poorly suited to the new challenge, the population has little capacity to adapt and faces a much higher risk of decline.
(d)(ii) One additional risk of low genetic diversity: continued inbreeding depression -- with little variation left, most matings are effectively between genetically similar individuals, so harmful recessive alleles keep being exposed in homozygous offspring, suppressing fertility and survival even without any new environmental threat.
